stemMd: A firm has $200$ employees. Of these, $120$ use the company gym, $85$ use the company pool, and $30$ use neither facility. How many employees use both the gym and the pool?
explanationMd:
Two overlapping groups plus a group outside both is the standard two-set count. Handle the outsiders first, because the overlap formula applies only to the people inside at least one set.

**Step 1 — how many use at least one facility?** Remove the ones who use neither:

$$200 - 30 = 170.$$

**Step 2 — apply the two-set rule.** For any two sets,

$$|G \cup P| = |G| + |P| - |G \cap P|.$$

Counting the gym users and the pool users separately counts anyone who uses both **twice**, so the double count is exactly the overlap. Substituting the numbers:

$$170 = 120 + 85 - |G \cap P| \;\Longrightarrow\; |G \cap P| = 205 - 170 = 35.$$

So $35$ employees use both.

**How to check the answer.** Rebuild the whole workforce out of four disjoint groups and see whether it comes to $200$:

- gym only: $120 - 35 = 85$
- pool only: $85 - 35 = 50$
- both: $35$
- neither: $30$

Then $85 + 50 + 35 + 30 = 200$. Every employee is counted exactly once, so the split is consistent.

**Why the four-group table is worth drawing.** It makes each wrong answer visible as a cell you have read off the wrong line: $50$ is the pool-only cell, $85$ is the gym-only cell as well as the pool total, and $30$ is the neither cell. Once the four numbers are written down, only one of them can be the answer to the question actually asked.

distractorRationale.a: This computes $120 + 85 - 200 = 5$, subtracting the entire workforce instead of the $170$ who use at least one facility. It quietly assumes nobody uses neither, which contradicts the stated $30$.
distractorRationale.c: This is $85 - 35 = 50$, the number who use the pool but not the gym. It answers "pool only" rather than "both".
distractorRationale.d: This is the total number of pool users, $85$, reported as though every pool user also used the gym. That would leave nobody in the pool-only group, which the other figures rule out.
distractorRationale.e: This is the total number of gym users, $120$, reported as though every gym user also used the pool. Since only $85$ employees use the pool at all, the overlap cannot exceed $85$, let alone reach $120$.

accessibilityText: A firm has 200 employees: 120 use the company gym, 85 use the company pool and 30 use neither facility. The question asks how many employees use both. Five numeric options are offered in ascending order: 5, 35, 50, 85 and 120.

provenance.notes: Original item. The figures were chosen so that all four cells of the two-set table are positive and distinct (85 gym only, 50 pool only, 35 both, 30 neither), so every named misreading lands on a different number and the overlap is forced to a single value.

independentSolve.workingNotes: At least one facility: 200 - 30 = 170. Using inclusion-exclusion, 120 + 85 - both = 170, so both = 35. Consistency check: gym only 85, pool only 50, both 35, neither 30, total 200.

review.notes: Author solved the item with the inclusion-exclusion rule and verified the result by rebuilding the workforce from the four disjoint cells: 85 + 50 + 35 + 30 = 200. The overlap is algebraically forced, so no second value is defensible; each other option was traced to a specific cell of the table or to omitting the 30 who use neither. Numeric options are ordered ascending as on the real exam. Awaiting blind independent solve before publication.
